name: Socket Outlet (3-Pin UK Type G)
tagline: The 3-pole interface that lets you plug in an appliance — and the reason your board has RCD protection.
terminals: Terminal L/N/E screw-block behind the face
parts: Shutter — blocks the live and neutral holes
Live/neutral pins — carry the working current
Earth pin — the longest, opens the shutter
Terminal block — live, neutral, earth lands
safety: A UK socket is fused or supervised by the consumer unit's MCB, and earth is mandatory for the circuit. Don't 'bridge' the earth with the neutral — the entire protective system relies on a solid earth return.

points.label: Shutter
points.detail: A sprung shield covers the live and neutral holes. It only opens when a plug's EARTH pin presses it — that's why the earth pin is the longest. Children's fingers or a stray screwdriver can't reach the live contacts.

points.label: Live / neutral pins
points.detail: The plug's L and N pins make contact here once the shutter opens. Live (right, shorter hole) and neutral (left) are the current-carrying pair — rated at the socket's 13 A and fused inside the plug for the appliance.

points.label: Earth pin
points.detail: Earth opens the shutter and connects the appliance's metal body back to the protective earth conductor (CPC). Never block the earth hole — a fault will then seek a path through you instead.

points.label: Terminal block
points.detail: Behind the face, three screw terminals: L (red/brown), N (black/blue), E (green/yellow). Strip ~10 mm, clamp firmly, and check the fixing screws retighten the cable in the standard orientation.

points.label: Faceplate
points.detail: The white outer housing holds the mechanism and screws to a back box. It also carries the permanent 'maximum 13 A' marking and (with a socket this deep) the identifying brand/part.

cutaway.alt: Cutaway of a three-pin socket outlet showing the sprung shutter plate, contact tubes, rear terminals and cable clamp

cutawayPoints.label: Shutter plate
cutawayPoints.detail: A sprung plastic plate sitting behind the live and neutral apertures. Something has to push it aside before a pin can reach a live contact, and pushing needs either the long earth pin or both the other pins arriving together — so a single object in one hole meets plastic, not brass.

cutawayPoints.label: Earth contact and pin channel
cutawayPoints.detail: The earth pin is the longest on the plug, so it enters first and leaves last, and its channel is the ramp that drives the shutter out of the way for the other two. It also means a plug is earthed before it is live — the whole reason the pin is longer.

cutawayPoints.label: Neutral contact tube
cutawayPoints.detail: A sprung brass tube that grips the pin along its length rather than pinching it at a point. Contact pressure is what keeps the joint cool: a tired tube that has lost its spring makes resistance, resistance makes heat, and heat is how a socket melts behind a faceplate.

cutawayPoints.label: Live contact tube
cutawayPoints.detail: The same sprung tube on the live side, fed from the ring or radial. Note what protects what: the socket is rated for the circuit behind it, while the fuse in the plug protects the flexible cord of the appliance — which is why a 13 A socket feeding a 3 A lamp flex is safe only because of that fuse.

cutawayPoints.label: Rear terminals
cutawayPoints.detail: Live, neutral and earth screws at the back, sized for the circuit conductors plus, where it is needed, a second earth terminal for the bonding tail to a metal back box. Terminals are where the two conductors of a ring land, so a loose one there puts the whole ring on one leg.

cutawayPoints.label: Cable clamp
cutawayPoints.detail: Grips the outer sheath so a tug on the cable is taken by the clamp and not by the terminal screws. It also stops the cable being drawn far enough into the box to strain the conductors, which is what pulls a socket earth loose over years of plugs going in and out.
